item.description:
US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler attacks, Rubio says

The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday.

"We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff."

His comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing multiple individuals attacking Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist with the Washington Post. Levine was one of at least two people injured in the Friday incident, which took place as Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians.

European ‌diplomats and a French mayor also were attacked in the occupied West Bank, Belgium's foreign minister said.

The US State Department, Rubio said, has inquired about the event that included Levine's attack. Rubio, who spoke to reporters before boarding a flight to Uzbekistan, said he expects to hear back from the US Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday.

Israeli settlers in the West Bank have been involved in at least 170 attacks on Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

Report by AFP

item.description:
Israeli protesters say 'they are conducting ethnic cleansing' in West Bank

A group of Israeli demonstrators gathered in Tel Aviv on Saturday to protest against Israeli settler violence targeting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, calling for an end to attacks and greater accountability.

"We're protesting for the Palestinians for their right to justice, for their right to equal rights before the law, for their right to have their own state. We are protesting against the, the actions of the settlers and the actions which hurts us most of our army that is protecting the settlers," Tel Aviv resident Miriam Hirschfled said,

"And, we're protesting against the occupation. We think it's a disaster for them, and it's disaster for us. There's no future. We don't see that there's a future for us or for them if we won't be able to have some justice and some peace in the area."

Another Israeli protester, Martin Goldberg, said:  "We are here this Saturday night as we've been here every Saturday night for the last four years to protest the policies of this government towards the Palestinian people. They're conducting a programme of ethnic cleansing out of the West Bank and, of course, the war on Gaza."

He added, "Yesterday we witnessed a brutal attack on the Washington Post journalist. Today we witnessed a brutal attack on European diplomats. And what I would like to tell you is that these attacks are nothing out of the ordinary.

"What is out of the ordinary is they attacked so-called VIPs. And this is why it's in the news, every single day these attacks are occurring if it's against the Palestinians themselves, if it's against peace activists from Israel and if it's against peace activists that come from abroad. And we are here to say that's enough, we do not approve and we will do everything in legal power to prevent that happening," Goldberg said.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran has presented a concrete seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, Press TV reported.

Speaking at the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad on Saturday, Araghchi said Tehran had conveyed the proposal through Qatar and is prepared to restore passage through the strategic waterway if the necessary conditions were met, the report said.

At the same time, Araghchi said that the United States cannot expect maritime security to return to normal while continuing to exert military pressure on Iran, blaming US and Israeli war on the country for disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Security cannot be restored by more of the same,” he said. “One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation to return to normal.”

Araghchi said Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding in Islamabad on June 17 and subsequently begun technical discussions with Oman to facilitate the safe passage of vessels.

But Tehran's repeated attempts to pursue negotiations in good faith were met with military action, he said, creating deep distrust in the prospects for renewed talks without credible guarantees against a recurrence.

Despite those concerns, he said, Iran had kept the door to diplomacy open.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Rubio says Russia sanctions pause to 'analyse' impact on global economy
item.description:
Rubio says Russia sanctions pause to 'analyse' impact on global economy

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump's waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to "analyse" their impact on the global economy and "even to the US economy".

Rubio said the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.

He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis.

"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices but on economies as well," he said.

US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia -- measures adopted by Congress last month.

The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump's executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions.

The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month.

Report by AFP

item.description:
Israeli military sat on distress calls about settler attacks for two hours, report says

The Israeli military sat on distress calls for nearly two hours as activists reported threats from settlers in the occupied West Bank, but took no action until the attack on diplomats and others was over, the Haaretz daily reports.

The report said that Israeli military operations room received reports about the threats and calls for help as early as 1 pm on Saturday. Yet the Civil Administration and troops on the ground were informed of the attack only around 3 pm, after the attacks had ended.

One activist accompanying local Palestinians reportedly sent the army a video and the exact location of the incident, warning: “At least seven masked settlers armed with clubs. Come quickly, very scary. They stole bags of olives from Palestinians.”

The military has opened a special probe into the sequence of events and why no action was taken in real time to prevent the violence, Haaretz reports.

Israeli rights group, Yesh Din, has said that it documented 377 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians from 27 September  to 10 October, adding an average of approximately 27 incidents of violence occurred per day across 162 Palestinian communities in the West Bank.

Of these incidents, 174 were directly related to the olive harvest, and soldiers were present in 25 percent of the cases.

"The lack of law enforcement against violent settlers and soldiers who attack Palestinian olive harvesters, damage olive trees, and steal the harvest indicates that the obstruction of the olive harvest is part of a broader, systematic Israeli policy aimed at inflicting economic and cultural harm on Palestinians and displacing them from their land," Yesh Din said in a statement on X.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Is sisterhood the secret to a long life? The Sardinian village that could hold key to women’s longevity
item.description:
Meet some of the elderly residents of Bolotana, in line to be the world’s sixth ‘blue zone’ for its high number of female centenarians

When Giovanna Marras opens the door to her home in Bolotana, a mountain village in central Sardinia, her eyes are bright with curiosity as she sizes up her visitors. Her sister, Mariangela, peeks out too, soon ushering her guests inside and handing out dishes of ice-cream. The sisters are full of life, talking animatedly. Giovanna is 101 and Mariangela is 99.

Sitting in their living room, Giovanna swiftly recaps her life story: she excelled at school before moving to Cagliari, the capital of the Italian island, at 18 to train as a seamstress. The sisters went on to run a successful tailoring business in Bolotana before travelling the world after retirement. Neither married.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina
item.description:
Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors, of varying popularity, gazed disinterestedly at the scene.

item.description:
US seeks 'verifiable commitment' Iran won't rebuild nuclear programme, Vance says

US Vice President JD Vance said Washington was focused on securing Iran’s “long-term” and “verifiable commitment” not to rebuild its nuclear programme, while claiming the US had “in some ways decisively won” the war against Iran and destroyed its nuclear programme.

Speaking at a town hall hosted by CBS News, Vance said the focus was on preventing Iran from rebuilding its nuclear capabilities in the years ahead.

“Not over the administration of Donald Trump… but five years from now, could the Iranians rebuild that nuclear arsenal? Could they try to rebuild that enrichment capacity?” he said.

Vance acknowledged that “gas prices are too high right now” but said they would fall once the US-Israel war on Iran “is over”.

He blamed Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on tankers for driving up prices, saying, “We’ve never had a situation like this” in which one country was “trying to completely choke off world energy supply”.

Vance claimed petrol prices would be “three times as high if it weren’t for the US Navy keeping oil and gas moving out of the Strait of Hormuz”.
